items.source: А кто не пьет, назови, нет, я жду!
items.reference: And who doesn't drink? Pray, tell me, name them!! Go on, I'll wait!

general.text: Эта реплика иллюстрирует склонность артиста Велюрова к сценической самопрезентации и высокопарной самодраматизации даже в моменты бытовых телефонных оправданий. Фраза стала универсальным культурным мемом для комичной защиты собственных слабостей и пороков.

items.candidate: And who doesn’t drink? Name one! No, I’m waiting.

issues.justification: The candidate preserves meaning and the teasing challenge, but it tones down the high-flown, self-dramatising theatricality that the analysis highlights. "Name one! No, I’m waiting." is more prosaic and less grandiloquent than the reference's heightened stagey voice.

items.source: А не хлопнуть ли нам по рюмашке?
items.reference: Shall we toss back a quick one?

general.text: Этот вопрос идеально передает сюжетную функцию Костика как молодого трикстера, провокатора и медиатора в коммунальной квартире. Пассаж примечателен тем, что мгновенно и с иронией снижает патетику предыдущего монолога Велюрова, переводя высокую драму в регистр простого бытового товарищества.

how about
we knock back a little one?

general.text: Одна из самых узнаваемых цитат фильма, функционирующая как повторяющийся рефрен. Она саркастически резюмирует нелепость тройственного союза Маргариты Павловны, Саввы и Хоботова, блестяще подчеркивая комический контраст между заявляемой интеллигентностью и реальным удушающим контролем.
general.nb: Things to avoid: using a literal noun-phrase structure (like "High relations!") instead of a natural exclamatory phrase.

items.candidate:
Elevated... elevated relations.
You’ll go begging through courtyards,
driven by cruel fate...
suffering from wounds of the soul,
you’ll call on death in longing.
Is that Camões?
No, that’s François Villon.
His Testament.
Did he die too?
Yes—he too was either stabbed or hanged.
My God... So all poets end up like that?
Almost.
Hey, Lev Yevgenich,
the Orloviches are here.
Alas...
Oh, cut it out.
I’m telling you—I can’t.
But she said you must come...
But what can I do—I’m busy.
Come on, that’s not nice—
you were warned this morning.
And this morning I said I couldn’t.
Sorry, Savva, but it’s odd.
So you’re not coming?
No, I’m not.
Should I tell her that?
Tell her that.
But you’ll upset Margarita Pavlovna.
Regrettably.
Not nice.
How wonderful—thanks to you
I understood there’s no need to fear living.
True—what’s there to fear?
And nothing should be put off.
Buried in stone ditches—
oh, we won’t return, alas...
That’s François...
No, that’s Rimbaud. Arthur Rimbaud.
Died in the 19th century.
Very talented and very unhappy.
Him too?
Yes—his leg was amputated.
Ah! They all must have made a pact.
Yes, you’re right—there’s some mystery...
Oh, your lips are trembling.
Want me to teach you a little polka?
You dance?
No—it’s an old French song,
very naive and very transparent.
I’ll sing it for you now.
Rose Muda—we’ve summed it all up.
Rose Muda—there’s nothing for us to do here.
Rose Muda—my hometown is waiting for me.
The hour of farewell, Rose Muda—
we’re going home.
We’ll wear neckties again.
Go home without a leave pass.
He’s peculiar, isn’t he?
Yes—there’s something genuine in him.
We’ll meet girls
and walk them home till dawn.
Rose Muda—schenkt mir der Herz und der Ja.
Rose Muda—frag du nicht mehr die Mama.
Rose Muda—glaub mir, arg der Dreh.
Well, what’s going on in there?
Ours are playing at a French life.
Yes, art is deeply in debt.
When will you be back?
I don’t know, my angel—
nights, as a rule,
are full of surprises, aren’t they?
Mark my words—one day your Kostik
will surprise you.
Arkady Varlamych, why aren’t you watching the film?
You’re a servant of the Muses.
I serve Mosestrada.
Mon papa, ne veut pas
que je danse, que je danse!
How wonderful!
Isn’t it lovely?
Yes!
They’re knocking. Knocking!
Knocking.
So what is all this supposed to mean?
Well...
The Orloviches are waiting.
Sorry, I don’t understand what that has
to do with me now?
Khobotov, that’s petty!
You know I always couldn’t stand them.
You’re blinkered by your prejudice.
Excuse me, I have no time for discussion.
I have guests.
Yes... and many of them?
That’s irrelevant.
Velyurov told me something.
She’s some kind of воспитательница.
Velyurov is a gossip.
Besides, it’s nobody’s business.
Oh, I see! A rendezvous?
Margo, enough. Please.
What did she find in you?
Sorry, but for all your infantilism,
for kindergarten you’re...
too bulky.
First of all, she’s a medical worker.
And second, I’m an adult.
You’re an adult?
Without me and Savva you’ll be lost.
Who knows, who knows...
Enfant terrible, wretched thing.
No, no, no!
Khobotov, stop yelling.
Well, hello!
Hi.
If I’m not mistaken... Raisa?
Lyudmila.
Yes... I thought so... Listen, my dear,
I wanted to say...
Lyudochka—not "my dear."
My name is Margarita Pavlovna,
until recently...
Lev Yevgenyevich’s wife.
We stopped being spouses,
but we remained close people.
So there’s nothing surprising
in my taking his interests to heart.
Please.
But that’s not what this is about.
You see, Lev Yevgenich has
certain little oddities.
He can’t concentrate.
Knowing we’ll have guests tonight,
he invites you without batting an eye.
Yes, yes—I’m leaving.
Lyudochka...
You’re terribly absent-minded!
Goodbye, my dear!
My dear! Lyudochka!
This is unbearable!
Khobotov, Khobotov, you’re ridiculous.
Why?
Why ridiculous? Suppose I fell in love.
You fell in love?
You aren’t capable of love—like all secret erotomaniacs.
I repeat: if you meet a woman
who inspires my trust...
and whom I can, with a clear conscience,
entrust you to—I’ll be happy.
Now get up, get up—let’s go.
It’s awkward in front of the Orloviches. Come on.
Turn around.
There’s no need for them to think
that in our family there are...
these petty-bourgeois cataclysms.
Oh... Lyova’s back...
* If you’re happy, or if trouble finds you *
* In the buzzing crowd *
* I’ve long been coming toward you *
* In the buzzing crowd I sing of you,
I hope and I wait *
One graver is not like another.
One thing is a spitzstichel.
And quite another—a volstichel.
I can’t agree—there’s a little something in it.
For relief work you use only the volstichel.
He’s a fanatic of his craft.
Achtung! I engraved champions’ names with it
back on sports cups.
Engraving the winners’ names
is work that demands self-denial.
Khobotov—that’s decadence.
That’s life.
One man wins cups,
another engraves his name on them.
I don’t know, Lyova, about self-denial—
the job doesn’t require subtlety.
It’s done with a spitzstichel.
That’s a healthy way to look at it.
Exactly—masters don’t overthink.
And the gravediggers in Hamlet?
Tradesmen.
Would you look at that! Imagine—here too
someone dumped a girl recently...
and they didn’t catch her.
She’s been on sick leave three days.
Pulled from competition.
"Labor Reserves" society.
Svetlana. Master of Sports.
Excellent backstroke.
You see—the house has finally acquired
a real man.
My Savva is a delight. I’m so happy.
Wonderful evening, wonderful.
Everything’s so interesting.
Still, I want you to understand.
I understand. I understood everything...
I’ve come alive.
C’est magnifique.
Au revoir.
Don’t you dare do without the rifflers
and scrapers—that’s the main thing.
My dear—he’s obsessed.
That’s his charm.
I’ll explain in a second
wo der Hund begraben,
that is, where the dog is buried.
I understand, colleague. I understood everything.
What is this.
Lev Yevgenyevich, be brave.
Be brave—I respect you. I bow to you.
Lev Yevgenyevich, you were magnificent.
My dear—take care of yourself.
What are you talking about?
Well, mein Freunde...
Au revoir.
Auf Wiedersehen.
Goodbye. Au revoir.
Goodbye. Auf Wiederkucken.
My deepest bow.
Savva, Savva. Lyovushka, Savva.
Elevated, elevated relations.

issues.justification: The candidate diverges dramatically from the source: instead of preserving the film's short, sarcastic recurrent refrain, it begins with a literal-sounding noun phrase ("elevated relations") discouraged by the analysis and then inserts a large unrelated block of dialogue/lyrics. This addition changes function and destroys the original repeatable ironic effect.

items.source: Живут не для радости, а для совести
items.reference: You don't live to be happy, you live to do your duty.

general.text: Данная максима вскрывает солдатский фатализм, практическую логику и бытовую прямоту Саввы Игнатьевича. Уникальность этой фразы в том, что она обнажает главный абсурд «заботы» Маргариты Павловны и Саввы: лишение Хоботова свободы и права на личное счастье подается ими как исполнение высшего морального долга.

items.candidate: People don’t live for joy—they live for conscience.

issues.justification: The candidate substitutes "conscience" for the stronger, duty‑oriented sense in the analysis (soldier's fatalism and moral duty). This shifts the meaning from living to do one's duty to living according to one's conscience, which weakens the intended pragmatic, duty‑bound tone.

items.reference: For the record: I am not the one who suggested it!

general.text: Моментальный ответ Велюрова на предложение выпить фиксирует его лицемерное, но обаятельное позерство. Эта фраза вошла в язык как идеальная формула снятия с себя ответственности человеком, который страстно желает поддаться искушению.

items.candidate: Note: it wasn’t me who suggested it.

general.text: Это хлесткое восклицание подчеркивает властный, императивный характер Маргариты Павловны, привыкшей раздавать приговоры. Комический эффект достигается за счет абсурдного использования нейтрального профессионального термина в качестве громкого домашнего ругательства.
general.nb: Things to avoid: using literal standalone nouns (like "Culinarian!" or "Chef!"), which don't sound natural in English for this context.

issues.justification: The candidate uses a positive-sounding phrase ("Culinary genius!") rather than the biting, mocking exclamation of the reference. While it can be read sarcastically, the register is less punchy and imperious than the original domestic put‑down.

general.text: Слово является отличным примером характерного для фильма «иноязычия как культурной игры». Использование немецкого словечка маркирует типаж Саввы как фронтовика-ремесленника и одновременно работает как комедийный знак его автоматической готовности подчиняться командам жены.
general.nb: Things to avoid: translating the word from German into English, which ruins the character's specific linguistic quirk.

items.source: Резать к чёртовой матери, не дожидаясь перитонитов!
items.reference: Cut it the hell out, don't wait for peritonitis!

general.text: Эта реплика представляет собой пик медицинского фарса в картине. Ее ценность заключается в резком словесном контрасте: тонкие душевные терзания Хоботова грубо обрываются радикальным хирургическим приговором, который оформляет его статус беспомощного пленника ситуации.

items.candidate:
Cut it out to hell.
Without waiting for peritonitis.

issues.justification: The phrasing "Cut it out to hell. Without waiting for peritonitis." is awkward and non‑idiomatic in English; it breaks the harsh, brusque medical imperative into stilted fragments. The intended blunt, surgical command is preserved but the wording is clumsy.

general.text: Регулярно повторяемая формула, служащая инструментом психологического подавления. Через эту реплику Маргарита Павловна постоянно утверждает свою властную позицию, обесценивая любые попытки бывшего мужа вырваться из-под опеки и выставляя его незрелым ребенком.

items.source: Это мой крест!!! И нести его мне!
items.reference: This is my cross to bear! And mine alone!

general.text: Блестящий образец манипулятивного поведения, где домашняя тирания маскируется под великое самопожертвование. Этот пассаж особенно силен тем, что Маргарита Павловна гиперболизирует свои мнимые страдания прямо на глазах у Людочки, чтобы запугать ее и сохранить абсолютный контроль над жизнью Хоботова.
general.nb: Things to avoid: translating literally as "This is my cross!", which improperly splits the English fixed idiom "a cross to bear".

items.candidate:
It’s my cross!
And I’ll bear it.

issues.justification: The candidate splits and literalises the idiom into "It’s my cross! And I’ll bear it." which reads less idiomatically than the reference's "This is my cross to bear!" and slightly weakens the manipulative, exalted tone called for in the analysis.

items.source: Я вся такая несуразная… вся угловатая такая… такая противоречивая вся
items.reference: I am so utterly awkward... just all sharp edges... so entirely contradictory!

general.text: Эта самохарактеристика стала классическим мемом, великолепно фиксирующим узнаваемый женский типаж. В ней метко высмеивается манерность, кокетливая неуверенность и наигранная психологическая глубина, что доказывает мастерство фильма в создании резко индивидуализированных речевых портретов.
general.nb: Things to avoid: translating «угловатая» literally as "angular", which sounds overly literal and confusing in English.

items.candidate:
Ah, I’m so awkward,
so angular...
So contradictory, all of me!

issues.justification: The candidate uses "angular" for «угловатая», which the analysis warns against as overly literal. The translation remains understandable and playful, but the lexical choice sounds awkward and less natural for the self-mocking feminine register the original conveys.
